analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of California desert as national parks, wilderness, and a new preserve.
analysis.headline: The House passed the desert protections 298-128 on July 27, 1994, then set its own bill aside in favor of the Senate companion, which became law that October.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill upgrades Death Valley and Joshua Tree from national monuments to full national parks with large boundary expansions, turns the East Mojave National Scenic Area into a new park unit, and designates dozens of desert wilderness areas off-limits to mining, mineral leasing, and land disposal. It preserves existing grazing, keeps utility and pipeline corridors open, and reserves federal water rights for the new wilderness. The House passed it by a wide margin, then tabled it so the Senate companion carrying the same protections could become law.
analysis.who_benefits: Hikers, campers, sightseers, scientists, and future visitors, who get permanent statutory protection for desert scenery, wildlife habitat, archaeological sites, and Old West historic sites instead of management that could shift with each administration. Native communities gain guaranteed access to the lands for traditional cultural and religious purposes. Local economies around the parks gain a durable draw for visitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, campers, and future park visitors

how_it_helps.text: Establishes Death Valley and Joshua Tree as national parks and creates a new Mojave park unit, putting the lands under the permanent National Park System instead of the looser monument and scenic-area designations they had.

Designates dozens of BLM and refuge wilderness areas and roughly 3.2 million acres of Death Valley wilderness plus nearly 700,000 acres in the Mojave unit, the highest form of land protection Congress can give.

Withdraws the protected lands from mining, mineral leasing, geothermal leasing, and disposal under the public land laws, and requires the Interior Secretary to validate mining claims before approving any work plan inside the new areas.

Guarantees Native people access to the parks and wilderness for traditional cultural and religious purposes, including temporary closures to protect the privacy of ceremonies, and reserves federal water rights for the wilderness.
Transfers about 20,500 acres to California's Red Rock Canyon State Park and establishes the Desert Lily Sanctuary.

analysis.who_pays: Hard-rock mining claim holders and companies, whose claims inside the parks and wilderness are withdrawn from new entry, subjected to validity reviews, and in the Bodie Bowl capped and conditioned. Off-road vehicle users lose motorized access on designated wilderness. Livestock permittees, utilities, and the military keep their existing uses, though with added oversight.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining claim holders and off-road users

drawbacks.text: Existing livestock grazing continues at current levels inside the wilderness areas and the new park units, so a commercial use is locked into the protected landscape rather than phased out.

The bill guarantees Southern California Edison, Southern California Gas, communications carriers, and mining-related companies their existing rights-of-way through the new Mojave park, and even allows transmission-line upgrades, with limits, inside park boundaries.

Title VIII reserves large tracts including the China Lake Naval Weapons Center for military use for 15 more years, and exempts the United States from liability for damages from nonmilitary activity on the withdrawn lands; off-road users also permanently lose motorized access in designated wilderness.

Lands the government acquires for the parks must be appraised without regard to the presence of endangered species, which can lower what sellers receive, and the Secretary must negotiate land exchanges that could hand federal land to a private landowner or the state in return for clearing inholdings from the protected areas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public gain is large and permanent: the biggest desert conservation designation of its era, converting patchy monument and administrative protection into full National Park System and Wilderness Act status across millions of acres. The costs fall narrowly on mining interests and motorized recreation, while grazing, utilities, pipelines, and military uses are largely preserved with conditions, so the bill's main tradeoff is deliberately weighted toward protection rather than extraction.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed its version 298-128, then immediately tabled its own bill and pointed to the Senate companion, S. 21, which carried the same protections into law that October.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Lehman of California introduced the bill on January 21, 1993, and it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee.
The committee reported the bill amended on May 10, 1994, after a 28-14 markup vote, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
On July 27, 1994, the House voted 246-179 to cut off debate and limit amendments, then passed the bill 298-128.
Immediately after passage, the House laid the bill on the table — meaning it set its own passed version aside — and directed further action to the Senate companion, S. 21.

The bill was amended as it moved, adding military land withdrawals for China Lake and Chocolate Mountain, a Bodie Bowl mining restriction, Buy American requirements, and a study for a Timbisha Shoshone reservation, and renaming the Mojave unit a National Preserve in the final version.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Park visitors and future generations gained when the protections became law. Mining claim holders and off-road vehicle users lost the access and entry rights they had pressed to keep, and grazing and utility operators came out whole.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Park visitors, not mining or off-road users

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill from committee on a 28-14 markup vote, steered it through the Rules Committee and floor debate, and moved to cut off debate on final day.

for.name: Rep. Richard Lehman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the California Desert Protection Act and recruited cosponsors across two years.

for.name: 111 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, 101 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator, author of Senate companion S. 21
for.what_they_did: Authored and steered the Senate companion carrying the same protections, which became the vehicle for enactment after the House tabled its own bill.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the California Desert Protection Act of 1994 into law in October 1994.

against.name: 122 of 178 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans voting no on passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 122 to 53, after 169 of 178 had voted against cutting off debate.

against.name: Rep. Randy Cunningham
against.what_they_did: Offered an amendment on the floor to strike the Mojave desert protections, which a perfecting amendment by Rep. Miller superseded.

against.name: Hard-rock mining interests
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against wilderness and park designations that would withdraw desert lands from mining entry and subject claims to validity review.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was 298-128, with 244 of 255 voting Democrats in favor versus 53 of 178 Republicans; the motion to cut off debate split even sharper, 241-10 among Democrats and 4-169 among Republicans.

industries.note: New parks and wilderness are withdrawn from mining entry, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, and no work plan can be approved until claims are proven valid; the Bodie Bowl is further restricted to valid existing claims. Claim holders lose speculative value, while the public keeps landscape and historic sites the bill found were threatened by mining pressure.

Wilderness designation bars motorized travel across vast stretches of the desert that were previously open to the public under multiple-use management. A minority of desert users loses access so the land remains unmechanized for everyone else.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utilities and pipelines
industries.note: The bill guarantees existing rights-of-way for Southern California Edison, Southern California Gas, and communications lines through the new Mojave park and permits transmission upgrades within set limits. Their corridors are locked into the protected landscape even as the land around them is protected.

Grazing continues at current levels in the wilderness areas and park units, and permit holders get priority if they want to sell base property to the government. The commercial use stays as long as it exists today.

Title VIII reserves China Lake, Chocolate Mountain, and El Centro for defense purposes for 15 more years, with added duties: fire suppression, decontamination programs, public warning of risks, and an environmental impact statement before renewal. The military keeps its ranges while accepting new environmental and public-safety conditions.

industries.industry: Private inholding owners (e.g., Catellus Development Corp.)
industries.note: The Secretary must negotiate land exchanges trading federal lands for the private and state school lands inside the new parks and wilderness, a chance for owners to swap hard-to-sell inholdings for marketable federal land. The public gets a cleaner consolidated park boundary in return.

National park status, visitor centers, and permanent protection raise the long-term value of the region's recreation draw. The bill's own findings cite millions of Americans already using these lands for hiking, camping, and study.
